title: Chicagohenge: How City Streets Frame the Equinox Sun
summary: Twice a year, something strange happens in downtown Chicago: the sun rises and sets exactly in line with the streets. The effect is called "Chicagohenge," named after Stonehenge, the ancient stone circle in England that also aligns with the sun. It happens around the equinox — this year on September 22 — when day and night are roughly equal. "In Chicago's canyon of tall buildings, especially in the downtown area, the sun will be framed by the rising sun, and the setting sun will be framed by those tall buildings," says Michelle Nichols, senior director of public programs at the Adler Planetarium in Chicago. The phenomenon works because Chicago's streets follow the cardinal points of the compass: north, east, west, and south. All you need, Nichols says, is a wide street running east to west — and maybe a bit of elevation. Denver is another strong candidate, according to Geoff Boeing, who chairs the Department of Urban Planning and Spatial Analysis at the University of Southern California. He has published a comparative analysis of U.S. cities' street grids. Chicago and Denver, he says, are faithful to the compass because of 19th-century planning that spread across the Midwest and Great Plains. Grids made it easier to buy and sell land — and to map railroads. Ancient cities did this on purpose. Tenochtitlan, the Aztec precursor of Mexico City, was "carefully planned with astronomical knowledge," a 2021 paper noted. "Even if we didn't do it intentionally, we're still getting the same side effects at least once or twice a year," Boeing says. As Nichols puts it: "We don't rely on these alignments to tell us things, but they are really great reminders that, hey, the sky really is still up there." So if you're in Chicago around the equinox, look down a long east-west street at sunrise or sunset. You might catch the sun perfectly framed between the buildings — a skyline-sized version of Stonehenge, happening right in the middle of the city.
why_it_matters: It shows that decisions made long ago about how a city is laid out — by surveyors, planners and railroad builders — still shape what millions of people can see today, and it proves that astronomy is happening above the traffic, not just in textbooks.

background_read: The equinox comes twice a year, once around March 20 and once around September 22, when the sun rises exactly in the east and sets exactly in the west. The name Chicagohenge borrows from Stonehenge (an ancient circle of huge stones in England, built thousands of years ago, that lines up with the sun on particular days of the year).

Chicago (a large city on the shore of Lake Michigan in the U.S. Midwest) rebuilt its downtown on a strict street grid after the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, which is one reason the alignment still works today. In the 1780s, the young United States government surveyed much of the Midwest and Great Plains into square-mile blocks so land could be measured, bought and sold, and railroads could be mapped on top of it.

New York City has its own version of this event, called Manhattanhenge, when the setting sun lines up with the east-west streets of the Manhattan grid. Modern cities rarely plan for the sun this way, which is part of why these accidental alignments draw crowds.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a free sky show for everyone
perspectives.description: Anyone standing on the right street can see the effect, with no ticket, equipment or training needed. It turns an ordinary commute into a shared moment, and it pulls people outside to notice the sky above their own city.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — it is an accident, not a monument
perspectives.description: Skeptics point out that Chicagohenge is a side effect of land sales and railroad mapping, not a design for stargazing. They warn that the hype can overshadow the bigger problem that light pollution means many city dwellers rarely see a real night sky at all.

perspectives.perspective: Analytical — a pattern that keeps repeating
perspectives.description: Urban planners note that grids spread across the Midwest and Great Plains in the 19th century for practical reasons, while the Aztecs laid out Tenochtitlan with astronomy in mind. Two very different motives produced a similar result, which suggests alignment with the sun is a common by-product of ordered city planning.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what modern cities should copy
perspectives.description: As cities rebuild and densify, designers could decide deliberately whether to preserve east-west sightlines and darker skies. The event raises the question of whether the sun should be treated as part of city planning again, rather than as a lucky leftover.
